record.paper_title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy: bridging mathematics and clinical translation
record.context_brief: Risks of maintaining high tumor burden
record.original_question: Do the adverse effects and risks of maintaining a relatively high tumor burden in adaptive therapy outweigh the benefits of stronger competitive suppression of resistant cells? For containment strategies that delay resuming therapy until sensitive cells create strong frequency-dependent and density-dependent suppression of resistant cells, how should models and trials balance prolonged treatment sensitivity against symptoms, biomarker accuracy and measurement frequency, additional cancer evolution under on/off therapy, new metastases, lesion-level heterogeneity across metastatic sites, quality-of-life costs, and disease-specific or drug-specific safety limits?

evidence.quote: 3.2 Do adverse effects of maintaining high tumor burden negate potential benefit?

The prostate adaptive trial does provide some evidence that prolonged sensitivity may outweigh adverse effects of maintaining high tumor burden, but the promise of being able to perpetually control each patient’s disease did not happen. Why not?

Yet, there are likely dangers associated with containment strategies aiming for overall high, and persistent tumor burdens. These fall into four important categories: 1) patients becoming symptomatic, 2) the ability of the biomarker to be sufficiently accurate and measurable frequently, 3) subsequent cancer evolution during the period of adaptive therapy, and 4) risk of new metastases.

As more clinical trials of adaptive therapy emerge from integrating mathematical models with clinical opportunity and need, it will be essential to consider the trade-offs associated with maintaining relatively large tumor burdens.

Balancing these costs and benefits will likely be disease and drug specific, and will require a continued lockstep between mathematical models and empirical studies, data and observations of patients.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider an adaptive therapy framework for treating a heterogeneous tumor composed of two cell populations: drug-sensitive cells S(t) and drug-resistant cells R(t), evolving according to competitive Lotka–Volterra-type dynamics

  dS/dt = r_S S (1 - (S + a_{SR} R)/K) - d(t) S,
  dR/dt = r_R R (1 - (R + a_{RS} S)/K),

where r_S, r_R > 0 are intrinsic growth rates, a_{SR}, a_{RS} > 0 are interspecific competition coefficients capturing frequency- and density-dependent suppression, K > 0 is a carrying capacity, and d(t) ≥ 0 is a treatment schedule that may be switched on and off. A "containment" (adaptive) strategy chooses d(t) so as to delay resuming therapy until S is large enough to strongly suppress R, thereby prolonging the period before resistance dominates.

Augment this baseline with the following clinically motivated risk components attached to maintaining a large total tumor burden N(t) = S(t) + R(t):

(i) a symptom/quality-of-life cost functional C_sym(N), increasing in N;
(ii) a biomarker model B(t) = f(S(t), R(t)) + ε(t) used (with sampling frequency Δt and measurement noise ε) to drive treatment decisions;
(iii) an additional evolutionary process generating new resistant phenotypes at a rate μ(N, d) that may depend on tumor size and on/off scheduling;
(iv) a metastatic seeding hazard λ_met(N) increasing in N, producing new lesions whose local (S_i, R_i) dynamics may differ across sites i;
(v) drug- or disease-specific safety constraints d(t) ≤ d_max and N(t) ≤ N_safe.

Problem. Within this class of models, determine whether and under what parameter regimes a containment strategy that maintains a relatively high but bounded tumor burden yields a larger expected progression-free survival (or other patient-centered objective combining survival and C_sym) than a maximum-tolerated-dose strategy that aggressively minimizes N. Specifically:

(a) Characterize the set of parameters (r_S, r_R, a_{SR}, a_{RS}, K, μ, λ_met, noise level in ε, sampling interval Δt, N_safe) for which the competitive suppression benefit of large S strictly dominates the cumulative risks (i)–(v).

(b) Derive optimal feedback controls d*(t) = d*(B observed up to time t) that balance prolonged treatment sensitivity against symptom burden, biomarker inaccuracy, ongoing somatic evolution under intermittent therapy, new metastatic seeding, and inter-lesion heterogeneity, subject to the safety constraints.

(c) Identify quantitative thresholds (e.g., on a_{RS}/a_{SR}, on μ, or on λ_met) that separate regimes in which containment is preferable from regimes in which aggressive cytoreduction is preferable, and discuss how these thresholds should inform the design of clinical trials of adaptive therapy.
artifact.status_search_result: This is a broad modeling and clinical-translation question about adaptive cancer therapy. Recent literature (e.g., Strobl, Gatenby, Brown, West, and collaborators, 2022–2025) continues to investigate the trade-offs between competitive suppression and the risks of maintaining high tumor burden, with partial results in specific models (prostate cancer adaptive trials, ovarian cancer ACTOv, etc.) but no general resolution of when containment outperforms aggressive therapy across the risk categories listed. The question remains open as a general modeling/clinical problem.

status_evidence.title: A survey of open questions in adaptive therapy
status_evidence.snippet: Lists balancing high tumor burden risks vs. competitive suppression as an open question for modeling and clinical trial design.
status_evidence.claim: The trade-off is posed as an unresolved question in adaptive therapy research.

status_evidence.title: Adaptive therapy: a tumor therapy strategy inspired by ecological and evolutionary principles
status_evidence.snippet: Reviews ongoing trials and modeling work; notes that optimal balance between containment benefits and risks of high tumor burden is unresolved.
status_evidence.claim: General trade-off remains an active open research area.
